chapters.title: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice

learn.hook: The school canteen has 50 hot samosas at break time and 120 hungry students in the queue. Who gets one? Welcome to economics!
points: Human wants are unlimited: as soon as one want is satisfied, new wants appear.
Resources such as land, water, workers, machines, money and time are limited, and most of them can be put to more than one use.
Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with our wants. Because of scarcity, every person, family, business and country has to make choices.
Economic goods are scarce and usually carry a price, like rice, petrol or a notebook. Free goods, like the air we breathe, are available in plenty and cost nothing.
Goods and services are made using four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.

example.q: Think it through: A very rich businesswoman in Mumbai can buy almost anything she likes. Does she face scarcity too?
steps: Scarcity is not the same as being poor. It means resources are limited compared with wants.
She still has only 24 hours in a day, so she must choose between a meeting, time with family and rest.
Her money is large but still limited compared with all the things she could want, so she must choose between projects too.
So scarcity touches everyone, rich or poor, and everyone has to make choices.
example.answer: Yes. Her time and even her money are limited compared with her wants, so she must also choose.

learn.reallife: Limited train seats during Diwali, water tankers shared by a colony in summer, and your own 24 hours split between study, play and sleep are all examples of scarcity.

games.title: Free good or economic good?
items: The air we breathe
Sunlight that dries clothes on the terrace
The wind that cools you on a beach
Bottled drinking water
Petrol for a scooter
A school notebook
A haircut at a salon

games.title: Factors of production and their rewards

quiz.q: What is the basic economic problem that every society faces?
options: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
Resources are unlimited but wants are limited
There is too much money in the economy
People do not want anything new
quiz.explain: Economics begins with scarcity: our wants keep growing, but the resources to satisfy them are limited, so we must choose.
steps: Asked: the basic economic problem of every society.
Human wants are unlimited: when one is met, new ones appear.
Resources like land, water, workers, machines, money and time are limited.
So wants are unlimited but resources are limited; the option with these reversed is wrong.
Answer: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
quiz.mistake: Reverses the idea and thinks resources, not wants, are unlimited

quiz.q: Which of these is a free good?
quiz.explain: The air we breathe is available in plenty and nobody has to pay for it, so it is a free good. The others are scarce and have a price.
steps: Asked: which item is a free good.
A free good is available in plenty and costs nothing.
The air we breathe fits this; biscuits, a bus ticket and cooking gas are scarce and have a price.
So the air we breathe is the free good.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything useful must be an economic good

quiz.q: In economics, what does 'scarcity' mean?
options: A good is not available anywhere at all
Resources are limited compared with people's wants
Only poor people cannot buy things
quiz.explain: Scarcity is about limited resources compared with wants. Even goods sold in every shop are scarce in this sense, because they cannot be made in endless amounts.
steps: Asked: the meaning of scarcity in economics.
Scarcity means resources are limited compared with people's wants.
It does not mean a good is missing from shops, or is cheap, or affects only the poor.
Answer: Resources are limited compared with people's wants
quiz.mistake: Confuses economic scarcity with a good being completely unavailable

quiz.q: A farmer in Punjab uses a tractor to plough his field. Which factor of production is the tractor?
quiz.explain: Capital means man-made goods, such as machines, tools and buildings, that are used to produce other goods. A tractor is capital.
steps: Asked: which factor of production a tractor is.
Capital means man-made goods like machines, tools and buildings used to produce other goods.
A tractor is a man-made machine used to grow crops.
So it is capital, not land, even though it works on land.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the tractor is land because it is used on land

quiz.q: What is the reward earned by labour?
quiz.explain: Workers earn wages (or salaries) for their physical and mental work. Rent goes to land, interest to capital and profit to the entrepreneur.
steps: Asked: the reward of labour.
Factors and rewards: land–rent, labour–wages, capital–interest, entrepreneurship–profit.
So labour earns wages.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rewards of the four factors of production

quiz.q: A village has one empty plot of land. It could become a playground, a vegetable market or a health centre. What does this show?
quiz.explain: The same resource can be used in different ways, but only one use can be chosen at a time. This is why choices are needed.
steps: Given: one plot could be a playground, a market or a health centre.
Most resources can be put to more than one use.
Only one use can be chosen at a time, so a choice is needed.
So this shows resources have alternative uses.
quiz.mistake: Misses the idea that one resource can serve several purposes

quiz.q: Which statement about human wants is correct?
options: Wants stop once a person earns a salary
Wants are the same for everyone
When one want is satisfied, new wants usually arise
Wants and needs mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explain: Once Meera gets a bicycle, she may want a helmet, then a better bicycle. Wants keep coming back and growing, which is why they are called unlimited.
steps: Asked: the correct statement about wants.
Human wants are unlimited: once one is satisfied, new wants arise.
Example: after a bicycle, Meera wants a helmet, then a better bicycle.
Answer: When one want is satisfied, new wants usually arise
quiz.mistake: Believes that wants can be fully and finally satisfied

quiz.q: Why does even a very rich person have to make choices?
options: Shops do not sell to rich people
Time and other resources are still limited compared with wants
quiz.explain: Everyone has only 24 hours in a day, and even large resources are limited compared with wants. So scarcity, and the need to choose, affects everyone.
steps: Asked: why even a rich person must choose.
Scarcity means resources are limited compared with wants, not being poor.
A rich person still has only 24 hours a day, and even large money is limited compared with wants.
So time and other resources are still limited and choices are needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks scarcity only affects people who are poor

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: "Why can't everyone just have everything they want? Why do we have to choose at all?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Our wants never end, but resources are limited. That is scarcity, so we must choose. Now I see why I cannot eat ten samosas!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but are there enough resources for all the wants? What does that force us to do?

revise.summary: Human wants are unlimited, but resources like land, labour, money and time are limited and have alternative uses. This scarcity forces everyone, rich or poor, to make choices.
focus: Explain scarcity as limited resources compared with wants
Tell free goods from economic goods
Name the four factors of production and their rewards
Why resources with alternative uses force choices
remember: Scarcity: resources are limited compared with our wants
Free goods (like air) are plentiful and cost nothing; economic goods are scarce and carry a price
Factors and rewards: land–rent, labour–wages, capital–interest, entrepreneurship–profit
Capital: man-made goods such as machines, tools and buildings used to produce other goods
traps: Scarcity is not the same as being poor or a good being unavailable
Don't reverse it: wants are unlimited, resources are limited
A tractor is capital, not land

topics.title: Opportunity cost: the price of a choice

learn.hook: You choose to watch a cricket final instead of going to your friend's birthday party. The match was free. Or was it?
points: Every choice has a cost, because choosing one option means giving up others.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. Only the next best option counts, not all the options together.
Opportunity cost is not always money. It can be time, fun, rest or a chance to learn something.
Good decisions compare the benefit of an option with its opportunity cost.

A production possibility curve shows the combinations of two goods an economy can make with its resources and technology. To make more of one good, it must make less of the other, and the amount given up is the opportunity cost.

example.q: Think it through: Arjun has a free Sunday evening. In order of his liking, he could study for Monday's test, play cricket with friends or watch a film. He chooses to study. What is his opportunity cost?
steps: List the options he did not choose: cricket and the film.
Find the next best of these. Cricket was his second choice.
Opportunity cost counts only the next best alternative, so the film is not added.
So the cost of studying is the cricket game he gave up.
example.answer: The game of cricket with his friends, his next best alternative.

learn.reallife: When your family spends savings on a new fridge instead of a holiday, or when a city uses land for a metro depot instead of a park, the option given up is the opportunity cost.

items.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best ___ given up.
Making a choice always means ___ something else.
Opportunity cost exists because resources are ___.
On a production possibility curve, making more of one good means making ___ of the other.

games.title: True or false?
items: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative, not every option given up.
We count only the single best option that was given up, not all of them.
A free movie ticket has no opportunity cost.
You still give up the next best use of the time spent watching the movie.
Opportunity cost can be time, not just money.
Time spent on one activity cannot be spent on another, so it is a real cost.
Scarcity is the reason opportunity cost exists.
If resources were unlimited, we would never have to give anything up.
A government that spends money on a new highway gives up nothing.
The same money could have been used for something else, such as hospitals or schools.
When making a choice, comparing benefits with opportunity cost helps you decide better.
This is the basic idea of a careful economic decision.

quiz.q: What is opportunity cost?
options: The price printed on a product
The total of all options given up
The value of the next best alternative given up
The profit earned from a choice
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost is what you sacrifice by choosing: the value of the next best option you could have had instead.
steps: Asked: the meaning of opportunity cost.
Opportunity cost = value of the next best alternative given up.
Only the next best option counts, not all options together.
It is not the printed price or the profit.
Answer: The value of the next best alternative given up
quiz.mistake: Adds up all the options given up instead of only the next best one

quiz.q: Kavya can go to dance class, attend her cousin's birthday party or play badminton. She likes them in that order and goes to dance class. What is her opportunity cost?
options: The birthday party and badminton together
quiz.explain: Her next best option was the birthday party, so that is what she gave up. Badminton was only her third choice.
steps: Given: her order of liking is dance class, birthday party, badminton; she chooses dance.
Options given up: the party and badminton.
The next best of these is the birthday party.
So the opportunity cost is the party; badminton is not added.
Answer: The birthday party
quiz.mistake: Counts every option not chosen instead of only the next best

quiz.q: A farmer's field can grow wheat worth ₹60,000, sugarcane worth ₹80,000 or vegetables worth ₹50,000 in a season. He grows sugarcane. What is his opportunity cost?
quiz.explain: Wheat at ₹60,000 is the best of the crops he did not grow, so it is the opportunity cost. We do not add the vegetables too.
quiz.mistake: Adds all the forgone options or picks the value of the chosen crop
steps: Options not chosen: wheat ₹60,000 and vegetables ₹50,000
Next best = wheat = ₹60,000

items: Sugarcane (₹000)
Wheat (₹000)
Vegetables (₹000)

quiz.q: Sana spends two hours playing a mobile game instead of revising for her science test, which was her next best choice. What is the opportunity cost of the game?
options: The cost of the mobile phone
Nothing, because the game was free
The two hours of revision she gave up
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost is not always money. Here it is the revision time, and the learning, that she gave up.
steps: Given: Sana plays a game instead of revising, her next best choice.
Opportunity cost need not be money; it can be time or learning.
She gave up two hours of revision.
So the opportunity cost is the two hours of revision, not the phone's price.
Answer: The two hours of revision she gave up
quiz.mistake: Thinks opportunity cost must always be paid in rupees

quiz.q: A factory can make 6 cycles and 20 fans, or 4 cycles and 30 fans. If it moves from the first combination to the second, how many cycles is the opportunity cost of the extra 10 fans?
quiz.explain: To make 10 more fans, the factory gives up 6 − 4 = 2 cycles. Those 2 cycles are the opportunity cost.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of cycles still made, or the fans gained, instead of the cycles given up
steps: Cycles before = 6, cycles after = 4
Cycles given up = 6 − 4 = 2

quiz.q: Rahul gets a free ticket to a three-hour film. Is watching the film really free for him?
options: Yes, because films have no cost
No, because the cinema loses money
No, because he gives up the next best use of those three hours
quiz.explain: Even without paying money, he uses three hours that could have gone to something else he valued. That is the opportunity cost.
steps: Given: the ticket is free but the film takes three hours.
Opportunity cost can be time, not just money.
Rahul gives up the next best use of those three hours.
So the film is not really free for him.
Answer: No, because he gives up the next best use of those three hours
quiz.mistake: Believes something with no money price has no cost at all

quiz.q: A city council uses a plot of land to build a parking lot instead of a park, which was the next best option. What is the opportunity cost of the parking lot?
options: The park that could have been built
The cars that will park there
The money paid for the parking lot
The road leading to the plot
quiz.explain: The park is the next best use of the land that was given up, so it is the opportunity cost.
steps: Given: the land is used for parking; the park was the next best option.
Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up.
So the opportunity cost is the park.
The cars parked or money paid are what is gained or spent, not given up.
Answer: The park that could have been built
quiz.mistake: Looks at what is gained or paid instead of what is given up

quiz.q: Why does opportunity cost exist?
options: Because scarce resources force us to choose between options
quiz.explain: If resources were unlimited, we could have everything. Scarcity forces choices, and every choice means giving something up.
steps: Asked: why opportunity cost exists.
Resources are scarce, so we cannot have everything.
Scarcity forces a choice, and every choice gives up another option.
So opportunity cost exists because of scarcity.
Answer: Because scarce resources force us to choose between options
quiz.mistake: Does not link opportunity cost to scarcity

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: "I picked mango ice cream instead of kulfi, which I like nearly as much. The ice cream cost money, but what else did it cost me?"
teach.praise: Chirp! The real cost of my mango ice cream is the kulfi I gave up, my next best choice. That is opportunity cost!
teach.nudge: But what did I miss out on when I chose the ice cream? Which other option was I giving up?

revise.summary: Every choice has a cost because choosing one option means giving up others. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, and it can be time, fun or rest, not only money.
focus: Find the opportunity cost from a ranked list of options
Work out opportunity cost in rupees or units given up
Explain that 'free' things still have an opportunity cost
Read a production possibility choice: more of one good means less of the other
remember: Opportunity cost: value of the next best alternative given up
Only the next best option counts, not all options together
On a production possibility curve, the amount of one good given up to make more of the other is the opportunity cost
traps: Don't add up all the options given up; take only the next best
Opportunity cost is not always money; it can be time
Don't give the value of the chosen option as the opportunity cost

learn.hook: Should India grow more rice or more cotton? Use more machines or more workers? And who gets what is made? Every country must answer these questions.
points: Because of scarcity, every economy, from a family to a whole country, faces three central problems.
What to produce and how much: which goods and services to make with limited resources, for example more food grains or more cars, more schools or more roads.
How to produce: which technique to use. A labour-intensive technique uses more workers, while a capital-intensive technique uses more machines.
For whom to produce: how the goods and services, and the incomes earned, are shared among people.

In a market economy, buyers and sellers solve these problems through prices. In a centrally planned (command) economy, the government decides. A mixed economy, like India, uses both markets and government.

example.q: Think it through: A women's self-help group in an Odisha village has ₹50,000 and 10 members. Which central problems must it solve?
steps: What to produce: should they make pickles, papads or both, and how many packets?
How to produce: should they make them by hand (more labour) or buy a machine (more capital)?
For whom to produce: who will buy the products, and how will the earnings be shared among the 10 members?
These are the same three questions a whole country faces, only on a smaller scale.
example.answer: What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

learn.reallife: When your family decides what to cook, whether to grind spices at home or buy them ready-made, and how to share the food, it is solving its own small 'central problems'.

games.title: Which central problem is it?
items: Should the country make more tractors or more buses?
Should a farmer grow cotton or soybean this season?
Should a bakery bake more bread or more cakes?
Should cloth be woven on handlooms or power looms?
Should a road be built with many workers or with big machines?
Should a factory use robots or hire more workers?
How should the profit of a cooperative be shared among its members?
Who should get the limited seats in a government hospital ward?
How should the national income be divided among different groups of people?

quiz.q: A textile factory is deciding whether to use more machines or hire more workers. Which central problem is this?
quiz.explain: Choosing between more machines and more workers is a choice of technique, which is the problem of how to produce.
steps: Asked: which central problem the choice of machines or workers is.
How to produce is about the technique: labour-intensive or capital-intensive.
Machines vs workers is a choice of technique.
So it is the problem of how to produce.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the choice of technique with the choice of goods

quiz.q: A country must choose between producing more wheat or more cotton. Which central problem is this?
quiz.explain: Deciding which goods to make, and how much of each, is the problem of what to produce.
steps: Asked: which central problem wheat vs cotton is.
What to produce is about which goods to make and how much.
Choosing between wheat and cotton is choosing which goods to make.
So it is what to produce.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the choice of goods with the method of making them

quiz.q: The problem of 'for whom to produce' is about:
options: How the output and incomes are shared among people
quiz.explain: 'For whom' deals with distribution: who gets the goods and services and how income is divided in society.
steps: Asked: what 'for whom to produce' is about.
It deals with distribution: how output and incomes are shared among people.
Machines are 'how'; crops are 'what'.
Answer: How the output and incomes are shared among people
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'for whom' is about choosing the product or the method

quiz.q: Why do the central problems of an economy arise?
options: Because resources are limited and have alternative uses
Because there are too many shops
Because people do not like to work
Because money is printed by the government
quiz.explain: If resources were unlimited, no choices would be needed. Scarcity of resources with alternative uses creates the central problems.
steps: Asked: why the central problems arise.
Resources are limited and most have alternative uses.
So an economy must choose what, how and for whom to produce.
Without scarcity, no such choices would be needed.
Answer: Because resources are limited and have alternative uses
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the central problems to scarcity

quiz.q: A labour-intensive technique of production uses:
quiz.explain: Labour-intensive means relying more on human workers, like making handloom sarees, rather than heavy machinery.
steps: Asked: what a labour-intensive technique uses.
Labour-intensive uses more workers; capital-intensive uses more machines.
So labour-intensive uses more workers compared with machines.
quiz.mistake: Confuses labour-intensive with capital-intensive

quiz.q: In a market economy, how are the central problems mainly solved?
options: By buyers and sellers through the price mechanism
quiz.explain: In a market economy, prices set by demand and supply guide what is produced, how and for whom.
steps: Asked: how a market economy solves central problems.
In a market economy, buyers and sellers decide through prices.
A central planning office decides in a command economy, not a market economy.
Answer: By buyers and sellers through the price mechanism
quiz.mistake: Thinks the government makes all decisions in every type of economy

quiz.q: What kind of economy does India have?
quiz.explain: India has a mixed economy: private businesses and markets work alongside the government, which runs some services such as railways and plans for public needs.
steps: Asked: India's type of economy.
A mixed economy uses both markets and government.
In India private businesses work alongside the government, which runs services like railways.
So India has a mixed economy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an economy must be either fully market or fully government-run

quiz.q: In a centrally planned (command) economy, who mainly decides what, how and for whom to produce?
quiz.explain: In a centrally planned economy, a government authority plans and decides how resources are used.
steps: Asked: who decides in a centrally planned economy.
In a command economy, the government plans and decides how resources are used.
Shoppers and private firms decide through prices only in a market economy.
Answer: The government
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the command economy with the market economy

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: "Our bird kingdom has limited seeds and twigs. What big questions must we answer before we make anything?"
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! What to make, how to make it, and for whom. Three questions, all because of scarcity. I will call a bird meeting right now!
teach.nudge: You told me one or two questions. But isn't there another question about who will get the things we make, or how to make them?

revise.summary: Because of scarcity, every economy faces three central problems: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. Markets solve them through prices, a command economy through the government, and a mixed economy like India uses both.
focus: Identify which central problem a given decision belongs to
Tell labour-intensive from capital-intensive techniques
How market, command and mixed economies solve the problems
Why the central problems arise
remember: Three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce
Labour-intensive: more workers; capital-intensive: more machines
Market economy: prices; command economy: government decides; mixed economy (India): both
traps: Don't confuse 'how to produce' (technique) with 'what to produce' (goods)
'For whom' is about sharing output and incomes, not choosing the product
India is neither purely market nor purely command; it is mixed

chapters.title: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market

topics.title: Demand and the law of demand

learn.hook: When mangoes first arrive in May they are costly, and your family buys just a few. By June the price drops and suddenly there are mangoes in every bag. That is demand at work!
points: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period of time. Wanting something without the money to pay for it is not demand.

Law of demand: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, its quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded. Drawn on a graph, it gives a demand curve that slopes downward from left to right.
Besides its own price, demand also depends on buyers' income, prices of related goods, tastes and season, and what buyers expect about future prices.
Related goods can be substitutes, used in place of each other (tea and coffee), or complements, used together (cricket bat and ball).

example.q: Think it through: In a Lucknow fruit market, buyers purchase 10 kg of mangoes a day at ₹100 per kg, 20 kg at ₹80, 35 kg at ₹60 and 50 kg at ₹40. What does this schedule show?
steps: As the price falls from ₹100 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity bought rises from 10 kg to 50 kg.
Price and quantity demanded are moving in opposite directions.
A lower price makes mangoes more affordable and makes them a better deal compared with other fruits, so people buy more.
This is exactly what the law of demand predicts.
example.answer: It shows the law of demand: as the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

learn.reallife: Big festival sales, cheaper vegetables at the end of the day in a mandi, and people buying more train tickets when fares are cut all show the law of demand.

games.title: Substitutes or complements?
items: Tea and coffee
Sugar and jaggery
Bus ticket and train ticket on the same route
Rice and wheat
Car and petrol
Cricket bat and cricket ball
Fountain pen and ink
Mobile phone and SIM card

games.title: True or false?
items: Demand means wanting something, even if you cannot pay for it.
Demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay.
Other things being equal, a fall in price usually raises the quantity demanded.
This is the law of demand.
A demand curve normally slopes upward from left to right.
It slopes downward, because more is bought at lower prices.
If the price of tea rises, the demand for coffee tends to rise.
Tea and coffee are substitutes, so some people switch to coffee.
An increase in income can increase the demand for many goods.
With more money, buyers can afford to buy more.
The demand for umbrellas is the same in every season.
Demand for umbrellas rises in the monsoon.

quiz.q: What does the law of demand state?
options: Price and quantity demanded rise together
Other things being equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises
Quantity demanded does not depend on price
Sellers supply more when price rises
quiz.explain: Under the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, provided other factors stay the same.
steps: Asked: the statement of the law of demand.
Other things remaining the same, when price rises, quantity demanded falls, and vice versa.
So price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
'Sellers supply more when price rises' is the law of supply, not demand.
Answer: Other things being equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises
quiz.mistake: Confuses the law of demand with the law of supply

quiz.q: Ritu really wants a laptop but has no money and no way to pay for one. In economics, is this demand?
options: Yes, if the shop has laptops in stock
No, because demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay
No, because laptops are free goods
quiz.explain: Demand means being willing and able to buy at a price. A wish without the ability to pay is only a desire.
steps: Asked: whether a wish without money is demand.
Demand = quantity buyers are willing AND able to buy at a price.
Ritu is willing but not able to pay.
So it is only a desire, not demand.
Answer: No, because demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay
quiz.mistake: Thinks a desire alone counts as demand

quiz.q: The price of tea rises sharply. What is likely to happen to the demand for coffee?
quiz.explain: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When tea becomes costly, some people switch to coffee, so demand for coffee rises.
steps: Given: the price of tea rises sharply.
Tea and coffee are substitutes: used in place of each other.
Some tea drinkers switch to coffee.
So the demand for coffee rises.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a price change of one good cannot affect another good

quiz.q: Cars and petrol are complements. If petrol becomes much more expensive, what is likely to happen to the demand for petrol cars?
quiz.explain: Complements are used together. Costlier petrol makes running a petrol car more expensive, so fewer people want to buy one.
steps: Given: petrol becomes much more expensive.
Cars and petrol are complements: used together.
Running a petrol car costs more, so fewer people want one.
So demand for petrol cars falls.
quiz.mistake: Treats complements as if they were substitutes

quiz.q: When the price of mangoes falls from ₹80 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity demanded rises from 20 kg to 50 kg a day. By how much does the quantity demanded rise?
quiz.explain: The rise is the new quantity minus the old one: 50 − 20 = 30 kg.
quiz.mistake: Gives the new quantity, or the change in price, instead of the change in quantity
steps: Old quantity = 20 kg, new quantity = 50 kg
Rise = 50 − 20 = 30 kg

quiz.q: The demand for umbrellas and raincoats goes up every July. Which factor explains this?
options: A rise in the price of umbrellas
quiz.explain: Demand depends on season and tastes, not just on price. In the monsoon more people need rain gear, even at the same price.
steps: Asked: why demand for umbrellas and raincoats rises in July.
Demand also depends on season and tastes, not just price.
July is the monsoon, so more people need rain gear even at the same price.
So the factor is season and weather.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only price can change demand

quiz.q: How does a normal demand curve look on a graph?
options: It slopes downward from left to right
It slopes upward from left to right
It is a flat horizontal line
quiz.explain: Because more is bought at lower prices, the curve falls from left to right.
steps: Asked: the shape of a normal demand curve.
More is bought at lower prices and less at higher prices.
So the curve slopes downward from left to right.
An upward slope is the supply curve.

topics.title: Supply and the law of supply

learn.hook: Just before Diwali, a potter in Kutch works late every night making diyas. Why does he make so many more now than in March?
points: Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a period of time.

Law of supply: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls, the quantity supplied falls. Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
Sellers offer more at higher prices because they can earn more profit and can cover the extra cost of making more. So a supply curve slopes upward from left to right.
Supply also depends on the cost of inputs (seeds, fuel, wages), technology, weather for farm goods, the number of sellers, and taxes or subsidies.
Stock is the total quantity a seller has. Supply is only the part of that stock offered for sale at a particular price.

example.q: Think it through: A potter offers 100 diyas a day when the price is ₹5 each, 200 at ₹10, 250 at ₹15 and 300 at ₹20. What does this show?

Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

topics.title: Market equilibrium: where demand meets supply

learn.hook: Nobody in the sabzi mandi announces the price of tomatoes on a loudspeaker, yet by mid-morning almost everyone is paying about the same price. Who decided it?
points: The market price is set by the meeting of demand (buyers) and supply (sellers).
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At this price the market 'clears': there is no extra unsold stock and no buyer left unable to buy at that price.
If the price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied is more than quantity demanded. This surplus (excess supply) pushes sellers to cut the price.
If the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded is more than quantity supplied. This shortage (excess demand) pushes the price up.
When demand rises (for example, sweets at Diwali) the equilibrium price rises. When supply rises (for example, a bumper harvest) the equilibrium price falls.

example.q: Think it through: Tomatoes in a mandi. At ₹20 per kg, buyers want 100 kg and sellers offer 40 kg. At ₹30: 80 kg and 60 kg. At ₹40: 60 kg and 60 kg. At ₹50: 40 kg and 80 kg. Find the equilibrium.
steps: Look for the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
At ₹40 per kg, both are 60 kg.
At ₹20 or ₹30 there is a shortage, so the price would be pushed up.
At ₹50 there is a surplus of 80 − 40 = 40 kg, so sellers would cut the price.
example.answer: The equilibrium price is ₹40 per kg and the equilibrium quantity is 60 kg.

learn.hook: Your pocket money is gone by the 10th of every month, and you cannot remember where it went. A budget is the detective that finds out!
points: A budget is a plan of expected income and spending for a period such as a week, a month or a year.
Income is the money coming in, such as a salary, pocket money, business profit or interest. Expenses are the money going out.

Fixed expenses stay about the same each month (rent, school fees, a loan instalment). Variable expenses change (groceries, electricity, outings). Needs, such as food, shelter, medicines and education, come before wants.
If income is more than expenses, the budget has a surplus. If expenses are more than income, it has a deficit. If the two are equal, it is balanced.
'Pay yourself first': set aside savings as soon as money comes in, then spend the rest. Tracking every expense shows where money leaks away.

example.q: Think it through: The Sharma family in Jaipur earns ₹40,000 a month. They spend ₹12,000 on rent, ₹9,000 on groceries, ₹5,000 on school fees, ₹2,500 on electricity and phone, ₹3,000 on travel and ₹2,500 on outings. Is their budget in surplus or deficit?

learn.hook: Put ₹1,000 in a bank and do nothing. A year later there is more than ₹1,000. Where did the extra money come from?
points: Saving means keeping aside the part of income that is not spent today, for goals such as education, a bicycle or emergencies. An emergency fund is money kept ready for sudden needs like illness or repairs.
Banks keep savings safe and pay interest. A savings account lets you take money out any time. A fixed deposit locks money for a fixed period and usually pays a higher rate of interest.
Simple interest is paid only on the original amount (the principal): Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time ÷ 100.
Compound interest is paid on the principal plus the interest already earned, so money grows faster over time. Starting to save early gives compounding more time to work.
Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. It lowers the purchasing power of money, so savings should ideally grow faster than prices rise.

example.q: Think it through: Isha puts ₹5,000 in a bank at 10% interest a year for 2 years. How much interest does she earn with simple interest, and with interest compounded yearly?

Year 2: 10% of ₹5,500 = ₹550, so she has ₹6,050. Total interest = ₹1,050.
Compound interest gives ₹50 more because in year 2 she also earns interest on the first year's interest.

topics.title: Financial literacy: borrowing, risk and staying safe

learn.hook: "Congratulations! You have won ₹50,000. Just share the OTP sent to your phone." Would you share it? A financially smart person never would!
points: Financial literacy means having the knowledge and skills to earn, spend, save, borrow and invest money wisely.

A loan must be repaid with interest. Banks are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and formal lenders such as banks and cooperatives usually charge lower interest than informal moneylenders. Borrow only what you can repay.
Higher returns usually come with higher risk. Spreading savings across different options (diversification) reduces risk: don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Insurance protects against big losses. You pay a small regular amount (premium), and the insurer pays if the insured loss, such as illness or crop damage, happens.

Stay safe: never share your OTP, PIN, CVV or passwords; banks never ask for them. You do not need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. Offers that promise to double money quickly are likely frauds. Report cyber fraud on the national helpline 1930.

example.q: Think it through: Rohan gets an SMS: "You have won a lottery of ₹50,000! Click this link and share the OTP to claim it." He never bought a lottery ticket. What should he do?
steps: He did not enter any lottery, so the 'prize' cannot be real.
An OTP is a secret code that lets someone approve a transaction from his account. Sharing it could let a fraudster take his money.
He should not click the link or share the OTP, and should delete the message.
He should tell a parent and, if any money is lost, report it quickly on the cyber fraud helpline 1930.
example.answer: Ignore the message, never share the OTP or click the link, tell an adult and report fraud on 1930 if needed.

learn.hook: Every summer, a family in a Himachal village watched extra plums rot under the trees. Their daughter saw something different: a chance to make jam. That is how an entrepreneur thinks!
points: An entrepreneur is a person who spots an opportunity, often a problem people face, and starts an enterprise to meet it.
The entrepreneur brings together the other factors of production (land, labour and capital), makes the key decisions and bears the risk. The reward is profit, but there can also be a loss.
Useful qualities include creativity, willingness to take calculated risks, decision-making, leadership and persistence, which means learning from failure and trying again.
Some entrepreneurs run small local businesses, some build fast-growing startups, and social entrepreneurs start ventures mainly to solve a social problem, such as clean water or low-cost learning.
Entrepreneurs create jobs, bring new products and services, raise incomes and help the economy grow. They become job creators, not only job seekers.

example.q: Think it through: Anjali sees that plums in her village rot every season. She uses her savings to buy jars and a stove, rents a small room, hires two helpers and sells plum jam in nearby towns. Where do you see entrepreneurship?
steps: Opportunity: she turned a problem (wasted fruit) into a product people would buy.
Organising: she combined land (the rented room), labour (two helpers) and capital (stove and jars).
Risk: her own savings are at stake, and she could make a loss if the jam does not sell.
Reward: if customers like the jam, she earns a profit and creates jobs in the village.
example.answer: Anjali spotted an opportunity, organised resources, took the risk and aims to earn a profit, so she is an entrepreneur.

learn.reallife: The neighbourhood tiffin service, the tailor who starts a small garment unit and a young engineer who builds an app for farmers are all entrepreneurs.

learn.hook: Most great startups begin with someone saying, "Why is this so difficult? There must be a better way!"
points: A startup is a young business built around a new or improved idea that aims to grow quickly and serve many customers.
It begins with a real problem. Talking to possible customers and studying the market (market research) tells you whether people truly need your solution.
Instead of building the perfect product at once, founders make a simple first version, a prototype or minimum viable product (MVP), test it with users, take feedback and improve it.
If feedback shows the plan is not working, founders may pivot, which means changing the product or the target customers.

A business plan explains the product, the customers, the costs, the price and the expected profit. Money can come from own savings (bootstrapping), family, bank loans, angel investors or venture capital firms. Investors usually get a share of ownership, called equity.

example.q: Think it through: Zoya's startup sells cloth bags. Each bag costs ₹30 to make and sells for ₹50. She sells 200 bags in a month and pays ₹1,000 rent. What is her profit for the month?
steps: Profit on one bag = ₹50 − ₹30 = ₹20.
Subtract the rent: ₹4,000 − ₹1,000 = ₹3,000.
A business plan uses such numbers to check whether an idea can pay for itself.

learn.reallife: School science fairs, college incubation centres and app ideas tested with a small group of users first are all ways young founders try out ideas before growing.

learn.hook: A potter from Gujarat, Mansukhbhai Prajapati, made a clay fridge called Mitticool that keeps food cool without electricity. Innovation can come from anyone, anywhere!
points: An invention is the creation of something new. Innovation is putting a new or better idea to practical use, as a product, a process or a way of serving customers.
Frugal innovation means creating useful, low-cost solutions with limited resources, like a clay fridge that runs without electricity.

Ideas can be protected by law: a patent protects a new invention (for 20 years in India), a trademark protects a brand name or logo, and copyright protects creative work such as books, music and software.

The Government of India launched the Startup India initiative on 16 January 2016 to support new businesses. Incubators and accelerators help startups with mentoring, workspace and contacts, and Atal Tinkering Labs let school students build and test ideas.
A startup valued at US$1 billion or more is called a unicorn. Many startups fail, and founders treat failure as a lesson.

example.q: Think it through: An engineer designs a solar dryer. Later, a startup in Maharashtra makes it cheaply and sells it to onion farmers so they can dry and store their crop. Which part is invention and which is innovation?
steps: Designing the new solar dryer is the invention: something new has been created.
Making it affordable and bringing it to farmers who use it is the innovation: the idea is put to practical use.
The farmers gain because less of their crop is wasted.
So innovation turns a good idea into real value for people.
example.answer: Designing the dryer is invention. Making and selling it for farmers to use is innovation.

learn.reallife: Paying a vegetable seller by scanning a QR code, booking a doctor's appointment on an app and using a low-cost water filter in a village are everyday results of innovation.

quiz.q: In which year was the Startup India initiative launched?
quiz.explain: The Government of India launched Startup India on 16 January 2016 to support and encourage new businesses.
steps: Asked: the launch year of Startup India.
The Government of India launched Startup India on 16 January 2016.
So the year is 2016.

quiz.q: What is a 'unicorn' in the startup world?
options: A startup that has closed down
A startup valued at US$1 billion or more
A startup owned by the government
quiz.explain: The term unicorn was used because such highly valued startups were once very rare.
steps: Asked: the meaning of 'unicorn'.
A unicorn is a startup valued at US$1 billion or more.
It is a business term, not about toys or closed firms.
Answer: A startup valued at US$1 billion or more

quiz.q: What does a startup incubator do?
options: Helps early-stage startups with mentoring, workspace and contacts
quiz.explain: Incubators support young startups so their ideas can grow into working businesses.
steps: Asked: what a startup incubator does.
Incubators help early-stage startups with mentoring, workspace and contacts.
They do not collect taxes or close businesses.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of frugal innovation?
options: A clay fridge that keeps food cool without electricity
quiz.explain: Frugal innovation creates useful solutions at low cost with limited resources, like the clay fridge.
steps: Asked: the best example of frugal innovation.
Frugal innovation: useful, low-cost solutions with limited resources.
A clay fridge that cools without electricity fits this.
A costly car, hotel or mall is not low-cost.
Answer: A clay fridge that keeps food cool without electricity
quiz.mistake: Thinks innovation must be expensive or high-tech

quiz.q: A company wants to stop others from copying its brand name and logo. What should it register?
quiz.explain: Trademarks protect brand names, logos and symbols that identify a company's goods or services.
steps: Given: the company wants to protect its brand name and logo.
A trademark protects a brand name or logo.
Patents protect inventions and copyright protects creative work, so neither fits.
Answer: A trademark
quiz.mistake: Thinks patents protect brand names
